newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia benchmark to boost secondary debt market.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia benchmark to boost secondary debt market.

text.p: A benchmark bond issue proposed in Malaysia's annual budget for 1996/97 will help activate the moribund domestic debt market, but more needs to be done to increase liquidity, analysts said on Thursday.
While the number of bond and other debt issues had grown sharply over the past five years, a secondary market has been virtually absent, they said.
The analysts said an active secondary debt market was necessary for Malaysia to achieve its target of becoming a regional financial centre.

"The goverment has now decided that in order to stimulate the secondary market, some form of benchmark issue needs to be made," C. Rajandram, Chief Executive of Rating Agency Malaysia (RAM) told Reuters Financial Television on Thursday.

In the annual budget last week, Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced that a series of bonds aimed at providing a benchmark yield curve would be introduced in the private debt securites market.
The government has said it will begin issuing the new bonds early next year.

A government-backed benchmark would provide a standard for the market against which other bonds could be priced or traded. This will prevent issues from being overpriced, as is happening at present, Rajandram of RAM said.
"At this point of time one cannot even draw a yield curve, because it is fairly distorted and not in line with the market because of demand-supply imbalance," Rajandram said.

The new zero coupon bonds will be issued by the Finance Ministry's holding company, Khazanah Nasional, in small amounts of 100 million to 200 million ringgit ($40 million to $80 million) for various maturities ranging from one to 10 years, the ministry's Secretary General Clifford Herbert said at the weekend.
The government was still working on the bonds, which could be used to finance privatised projects, Herbert said.

Malaysia's bond market was underdeveloped mainly due to a declining supply of tradeable government paper as a result of the Federal Government's budget surpluses and the absence of secondary trading in the domestic bond market, Herbert said.
But fast-growing Malaysia, with its large privatised, infrastructure projects, had investment needs that required substantial funding from the debt market, analysts said.
The government has estimated that Malaysia needed some 536 billion ringgit ($212 billion) over the next five years to fund the large number of projects in the private and public sector.
During 1991 to 1995, funds raised in the bond market increased by 21 percent to 32.4 billion ringgit ($13 billion) over the previous five-year period.
However, in 1995, trade in medium- and long-term bonds only totalled 4.6 billion ringgit, or 23 percent of the total bonds issued.
"Funds like the EPF (Employees Provident Fund) buy high-yield bonds in bulk and keep them to maturity without trading them," said a bond dealer with a Malaysian bank.
"The bonds that are available are at such a low yield, sometimes 50 to 100 basis points lower than the market that they are just not worth it," he said.
The liquidity problem could be partly solved by allowing short sales in bonds. "We need to be able to short sell a bond to create a true benchmark yield," the dealer said.

Analysts said in addition, investment rules for funds like the EPF, National Savings Bank and Social Security Organisation, the cost of issuing debt instruments and laws governing the issuance process should be eased to promote wider participation.
At present, almost all issues are done on a bought deal basis with the final number of investors limited to around 10 to 15.
- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
($1 = 2.52 ringgit)
